extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students and mathematicians interested in elegant proofs and classical results
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply classical theorem statements, proof techniques, and accompanying facts from an advanced undergraduate/graduate-level mathematics textbook (Aigner & Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK). Includes analysis in analysis, combinatorics, and probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 2 (Pólya-style covering for monic real-root polynomials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let p(x) be a real polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 with leading coefficient 1, and all roots real. Then the set P = {x ∈ R : |p(x)| ≤ 2} can be covered by intervals of total length at most 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: arrange the components I1,...,It of P, show each interval contains a root, partition p(x)=q(x)r(x) according to roots in the rightmost interval, form p1(x)=q(x+d)r(x) to shift roots and merge intervals, iterate at most t−1 times to obtain a monic polynomial p˜ whose sublevel set 'P is a single interval with length at least the total length of P; apply corollary of Chebyshev to bound length ≤4. Includes the explicit constructive shifting argument and the use of continuity and finiteness of level crossings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev's Theorem (monic polynomial uniform lower bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let p(x) be a real polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 with leading coefficient 1. Then max_{−1≤x≤1} |p(x)| ≥ 1/2^{n−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality characterization: the unique monic polynomial attaining equality is (1/2^{n−1}) T_n(x) where T_n(x)=cos(nθ), x=cos θ (Chebyshev polynomials). Proof structure: substitute x = cos θ to obtain g(θ)=p(cos θ), represent g as a cosine polynomial of order n with leading coefficient b_n = 1/2^{n−1}, then show for any cosine polynomial h of order n the highest coefficient magnitude |λ_n| ≤ max|h(θ)| by sampling at θ = kπ/n and a root-counting contradiction. Used to deduce interval-length corollary by affine rescaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary (interval length from Chebyshev)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p(x) is a real monic polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 and |p(x)| ≤ 2 for all x in [a,b], then b − a ≤ 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: affine change of variables sending [a,b] to [−1,1] produces q(y)=p((b−a)/2 (y+1)+a) with leading coefficient ((b−a)/2)^n; apply Chebyshev's theorem to get 2 ≥ ((b−a)/2)^n (1/2^{n−1}) = 2 ( (b−a)/4 )^n, hence b−a ≤4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact 1 (multiple root of derivative implies root of polynomial)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p(x) is a non-constant polynomial with only real roots and b is a multiple root of p′(x), then b is also a root of p(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via factorization p(x)=∏_{j=1}^r (x−b_j)^{s_j}: multiplicity bookkeeping shows multiple roots of p′ can only occur among roots of p(x); uses degree count of p′ and locations of simple roots between consecutive roots of p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact 2 (inequality for polynomials with real roots)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p(x) is a polynomial with only real roots, then p′(x)^2 ≥ p(x) p′′(x) for all x ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: use logarithmic derivative p′/p = ∑_{k=1}^n 1/(x−a_k) and differentiate again to obtain (p′′ p − p′^2)/p^2 = −∑_{k=1}^n 1/(x−a_k)^2 < 0, hence p′^2 ≥ p p′′; trivial at roots of p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Littlewood–Offord lemma (original statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a_1,...,a_n be complex numbers with |a_i| ≥ 1 for all i. Consider the 2^n sums ∑_{i=1}^n ε_i a_i with ε_i ∈ {1,−1}. Then the number of those sums which lie in the interior of any circle of radius 1 is not greater than c·2^n / (√n log n) for some constant c>0 (Littlewood–Offord, 1943).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: Erdős improved the bound by removing the log n factor (to order 2^n/√n); for real a_i the exact combinatorial bound equals the central binomial coefficient via Sperner's theorem. The text explains the reduction to Sperner for real positive a_i by mapping sign choices to subsets I = {i: ε_i=1} and observing the collection of I is an antichain if all sums lie in an interval of length 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner's Theorem (used as combinatorial tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any antichain (family of pairwise incomparable subsets) of subsets of an n-set has size at most binom(n, ⌊n/2⌋).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to bound the number of ± combinations falling into a small region (interval/circle) by mapping sign patterns to subsets and showing they form an antichain; invoke Stirling's formula for asymptotic estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős observation for real coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For real (in fact positive) a_i with |a_i| ≥ 1, the number of ± combinations ∑ ε_i a_i lying in an interval of length 2 is at most binom(n, ⌊n/2⌋).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: transform each signed sum to the subset I of indices with ε_i = 1; if I ⊂ I′ then the difference of sums is at least 2, contradiction, hence the family of I is an antichain and apply Sperner's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleitman's theorem (Hilbert-space/general vector version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a_1,...,a_n be vectors in R^d, each of length at least 1, and let R_1,...,R_k be k open regions of R^d where |x − y| < 2 for any x,y in the same region R_i. Then the number of linear combinations ∑_{i=1}^n ε_i a_i (ε_i ∈ {1,−1}) that can lie in the union ⋃_i R_i is at most the sum of the k largest binomial coefficients binom(n,j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, for k=1 this yields the binomial central bound binom(n, ⌊n/2⌋). Proof outline: assume regions disjoint, use recursion/induction on n along with the binomial recursion and a geometric translation argument (claim: one translated region R_j − a_n is disjoint from all R_i + a_n) to split combinations into two classes mapped to combinations for n−1 vectors lying in k+1 or k−1 regions respectively; apply induction and the combinatorial identity for sums of largest binomial coefficients. The bound is tight for identical vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler/Herglotz cotangent partial fraction expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: For x ∈ R\Z, π cot(π x) = 1/x + ∑_{n=1}^∞ (1/(x+n) + 1/(x−n)). Equivalently π cot(π x) = lim_{N→∞} ∑_{n=−N}^N 1/(x+n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation via Herglotz trick: define f(x)=π cot πx and g(x)=lim_{N→∞} ∑_{n=−N}^N 1/(x+n), show f and g are continuous off integers, periodic of period 1, odd, satisfy the same functional equation f(x/2)+f((x+1)/2)=2f(x) (and same for g), and their difference extends continuously to R with value 0 at integers; maximum principle/iteration implies identity. Also rewrite as π cot πx = 1/x − ∑_{n=1}^∞ 2x/(n^2−x^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bernoulli numbers and Euler's formula for ζ(2k)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power series expansion of y cot y yields the relation between Bernoulli numbers B_{2k} and the zeta values: ζ(2k) = (−1)^{k−1} 2^{2k−1} B_{2k} π^{2k} / (2k)! (equivalently the formula given in the text linking coefficients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: expand y cot y via exponential generating series z/(e^z − 1) and identify coefficients; combine with the partial fraction expansion to equate coefficients of y^{2k}, yielding the closed forms for ζ(2k). Table of first Bernoulli numbers and sample values ζ(2)=π^2/6, ζ(4)=π^4/90, etc., given; remarks about growth of |B_{2k}| and appearance of primes in numerators (e.g., 691).

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffon's needle theorem (short-needle probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a short needle of length ℓ (ℓ ≤ d) is dropped on paper ruled by parallel lines distance d apart, then the probability that the needle crosses a line is p = (2/π) (ℓ/d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs given: (1) Barbier's Book Proof via linearity of expectation: expected number of crossings E(ℓ) satisfies E(x+y)=E(x)+E(y) hence E(ℓ)=cℓ; drop a circular needle (diameter d) which always produces exactly two intersections to deduce c = 2/(π d) and so p = E(ℓ) = (2/π)(ℓ/d). (2) Calculus/geometry proof: average the crossing probability ℓ sin α / d over angles α ∈ [0,π/2] to obtain same value. Historical note on Lazzarini's suspicious experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffon's needle general formula (long needles)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a needle of length ℓ ≥ d the probability of crossing is given by evaluating integrals splitting at α = arcsin(d/ℓ): p = (2/π) [ ∫_0^{arcsin(d/ℓ)} (ℓ sin α)/d dα + ∫_{arcsin(d/ℓ)}^{π/2} 1 dα ], resulting in an explicit (but less tidy) expression depending on ℓ/d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: the formula reduces to (2/π)(ℓ/d) at ℓ=d, is strictly increasing in ℓ, and tends to 1 as ℓ→∞. The text suggests as an exercise to verify these properties from the explicit expression (which contains arcsin(d/ℓ) and a sqrt(1−d^2/ℓ^2) term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeon-hole principle (basic and quantitative form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n objects are placed in r boxes with r < n, then at least one box contains more than one object. Quantitatively, there exists a box containing at least ⌈n/r⌉ objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping formulation: for finite sets N (|N|=n) and R (|R|=r) and mapping f:N→R there exists a ∈ R with |f^{-1}(a)| ≥ ⌈n/r⌉. Simple counting proof given; used throughout the combinatorial applications in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility claim in {1,...,2n}
rubrics_metrics.description: From any subset A ⊆ {1,2,...,2n} with |A| = n+1 there exist two numbers in A such that one divides the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write each a ∈ A as a = 2^k m with m odd (1 ≤ m ≤ 2n−1). There are only n possible odd parts, so two numbers share the same odd part; the larger is a multiple of the smaller by a power of 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatively prime adjacent-pair claim in {1,...,2n}
rubrics_metrics.description: From any n+1 numbers chosen among 1,2,...,2n there are two which are relatively prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple observation: among n+1 chosen numbers from 1..2n there must be two consecutive integers (pigeonhole on pairs), and consecutive integers are relatively prime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequence theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: In any sequence a_1, a_2, ..., a_{mn+1} of mn+1 distinct real numbers, there exists either an increasing subsequence of length m+1 or a decreasing subsequence of length n+1 (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via pigeonhole: assign to each a_i the length t_i of the longest increasing subsequence starting at a_i. If any t_i ≥ m+1 we are done; otherwise t_i ∈ {1,...,m} and by pigeonhole some value s occurs at least n+1 times, and those corresponding elements form a decreasing subsequence. The statement is sharp for mn elements (counterexamples exist).
